codes.title: markless-allow cannot suppress errors
codes.message: markless-allow named <code>, but <errorCode> is an error and must still be fixed.
codes.why: markless-allow is a per-site escape hatch for warning diagnostics only; it must stay readable and current for the next person editing the site.
codes.suggestion: Fix the diagnostic or remove the markless-allow comment.

codes.title: markless-allow needs a reason
codes.message: Use `// markless-allow CODE: reason`; for this site, write `// markless-allow <code>: reason`.
codes.why: markless-allow is a per-site escape hatch for warning diagnostics only; it must stay readable and current for the next person editing the site.
codes.suggestion: // markless-allow CODE: reason

codes.title: markless-allow did not match this site
codes.message: markless-allow named <code>, but that diagnostic did not fire at this site.
codes.why: markless-allow is a per-site escape hatch for warning diagnostics only; it must stay readable and current for the next person editing the site.
codes.suggestion: Fix the diagnostic or remove the markless-allow comment.

settled with rendered @try/@catch content, but this host provides no HTML renderer to build DOM nodes from it.

codes.title: Delegate child prop is not build-known
codes.message: MARKLESS_ARTIFACT_CHILD_PROP_NOT_BUILD_KNOWN: <<componentName>> prop <prop> must be a build-known static value. Runtime component execution is not a fallback.
codes.why: A delegate is rendered once at build time, so every prop it reads must be a value the compiler can read at build time.
codes.suggestion: Pass a static value, or compose the child as TSRX source.

codes.title: Delegate child renderSsr returned no static HTML
codes.message: MARKLESS_ARTIFACT_CHILD_RENDER_INVALID: <<componentName>> renderSsr must return static HTML.
codes.why: The materialized edge is the delegate rendered output, so an output without HTML leaves nothing to inline.
codes.suggestion: Return an object with a string `html` field from renderSsr.

codes.title: The settled @try content cannot render in the browser yet
codes.why: The compiler emits a browser-side render module for @try/@catch content so it can update after the data settles. A shape the module cannot render would silently stay frozen, so the compiler reports it instead.

codes.title: Async computed reads need an async boundary
codes.message: Cannot read <computedLabel> "<source>" outside @try/@pending/@catch. Wrap the read in an async boundary.
codes.why: Async computed values can be pending or rejected during initial render and resume. The runtime needs an explicit TSRX async boundary to render pending and error UI.
codes.suggestion: Wrap this template read in @try with @pending and @catch branches, or read a sync computed that is already guarded by an async boundary.

codes.title: Reactive reads after await are not resumable
codes.message: Cannot read "<source>" after await in async computed "<computedName>". Snapshot the value before awaiting.
codes.why: Async computed dependency keys are captured before the first await. Reading graph state after suspension would make revalidation and resume depend on hidden async timing.
codes.suggestion: Read the graph value before the first await, or split post-await formatting into a separate sync computed().

codes.title: attach can only be bound to host elements
codes.message: Cannot bind attach={<source>} on component <owner>. attach installs DOM behavior and needs a concrete host element owner.
codes.why: Element behaviors are resumed by locating the owning DOM element. A component is not a DOM locator and may render zero, one, or many host nodes.
codes.suggestion: Move attach={...} to a host element such as <canvas>, or make the component forward behavior to a known host element in its own TSRX body.

codes.title: Duplicate attribute on one element
codes.message: `<attributeName>` appears twice on <tag>. Only one can win, and render paths can disagree about which value is used.
codes.why: Duplicate attributes ship invalid HTML and make the element depend on parser and update semantics instead of one authored value.
codes.suggestion: Keep one `<attributeName>` attribute on this element.

codes.title: Lowercase on* attributes are plain HTML attributes
codes.message: `<attributeName>={<valueSource>}` is a plain attribute, not a Markless event. It would serialize the function source into HTML.<eventText>
codes.why: Attribute bindings serialize to plain text in HTML and DOM updates; only graph cells keep structured values across resume.
codes.suggestion: Use the event prop casing, for example `<eventSuggestion>={...}`, or serialize a string deliberately.

codes.title: A branch arm renders a bare expression instead of a fragment
codes.message: `{<expressionSource>}` stands alone as this arm's whole body. A standalone expression container is not a template output node, so the arm has no markup of its own and its text has nowhere to live but the element around it — which erases whatever the other arm rendered there.
codes.why: Template output is an element, a fragment, or a control-flow construct. A statement container that needs to render text says so with a fragment, which gives the text its own marker range inside the arm.
codes.suggestion: Wrap it in a fragment: <wrapped>

codes.title: This element behavior cannot run in the browser yet
codes.message: Cannot emit lazy behavior symbol "<symbolId>" because it reads component-local "<name>", a local <bindingKindLabel> value that cannot cross a resume boundary.
codes.why: Element behavior symbols run after browser resume. Behavior factories may use module functions, graph inputs, element handles, props/shared values, or serializable capture-plane inputs; unsupported body locals would otherwise become missing behavior code.

codes.message: Branch <id> resolved arm <arm> to an empty fragment.

codes.title: Changing this <label> cannot rebuild what it shows
codes.message: this <label> (<testSource>) cannot be rebuilt when <testSource> changes because <detail>.
codes.why: Showing or hiding this content replaces it wholesale from compiled markup plus value reads. A component is rebuilt from the markup its own file compiled, so one that brings state of its own, shows a function it was handed, or — when it comes from another file — shows a value that keeps changing while it is shown has nothing left to be rebuilt from, and the browser would ask for code the build never wrote. That failure stops every other update in the same component.
codes.suggestion: Move the component outside the <label> and hide it with an attribute, lift its state up to the component that owns the <label>, or keep the <label> content to plain elements, text, and state reads.

codes.title: A branch alternative is spelled `else` instead of `@else`
codes.message: This `else` follows an @if arm but is not written as `@else`, so it is not read as a branch at all. TSRX parses it as literal text next to the @if, and the block after it becomes a separate expression, so the page renders the word "else" followed by the arm's own source as escaped text.
codes.why: Markless branches are spelled with the `@` sigil — `@if`, `@else if`, `@else` — because that sigil is what tells the parser a construct starts here. Without it the parser has no branch to attach the alternative to, and the mistake is silent: the module compiles and ships visible garbage instead of failing.
codes.suggestion: Write the alternative as `@else { ... }`.

codes.title: Callback props accept at most one parameter
codes.message: Callback prop `<propName>` is unsupported because <value>. Lazy callback symbols accept zero parameters or one simple identifier, object pattern, or array pattern without top-level defaults or rest.
codes.why: The callback transport carries one callback value across the lazy-symbol boundary. Multiple parameters, defaults, and rest bindings do not have supported parameter semantics when the symbol runs.
codes.suggestion: Pass a single object instead — change `(kind, payload) => ...` to `({ kind, payload }) => ...` and invoke the callback with one object value; remove parameter defaults and rest bindings.

codes.title: A callback slot can only be filled by the widget root’s own callback prop
codes.message: "<componentName>" assigns <valueSource> into the "<slotName>" callback slot of shared() "<definitionName>", and <valueSource> is not one of this component's callback props.
codes.why: A callback slot is a compile-time route, not a stored value: the build records that this widget root’s callback prop answers the slot, and a part invoking the slot dispatches straight to the consumer’s handler. A local function has no consumer to route to, so nothing could be recorded and the call would silently do nothing.
codes.suggestion: Declare the handler as a prop of <componentName> and assign that prop: <slotName> = <thatProp>.

codes.title: A callback slot is invoked but no component fills it
codes.message: shared() "<definitionName>" invokes its "<slotName>" callback slot, but no component in this module assigns a callback prop into it.
codes.why: Without an assignment there is no widget root to route the call to, so the invocation can never reach a consumer and does nothing at runtime.
codes.suggestion: Assign the widget root's callback prop into the slot: <instance>.<slotName> = <thatProp>.

codes.message: <graphNodeId> was dispatched from a part whose widget instance no rendered widget owns, so the consumer's callback could never be reached.

codes.title: Imported child has no current capture metadata
codes.message: MARKLESS_CAPTURE_METADATA_MISSING: Parent module <parent> composes imported child <specifier>, but its compiled artifact has no current capture metadata. Rebuild the child with the current Markless compiler and clear any stale build cache.
codes.why: Composing a child whose capture metadata is stale or absent would link captures against an artifact this compiler did not produce.
codes.suggestion: Rebuild the child with the current Markless compiler and clear any stale build cache.

codes.title: Lazy handler prop capture is not resumable
codes.message: Cannot bind lazy symbol "<symbolId>" on component edge "<componentEdgeId>" because prop "<propName>" is not passed by the parent that renders "<componentName>", and this call site invokes it unconditionally.
codes.why: An absent prop has no value to route at this component edge. An optional or guarded call folds to undefined; an unconditional call would throw after resume, so it stays a build error.
codes.suggestion: Call it optionally as <propName>?.(…), guard it with if (<propName>), or pass <propName> where "<componentName>" is rendered.

codes.title: Cannot capture local <bindingKindLabel> in lazy symbol
codes.message: Cannot capture "<name>" in lazy <kind> symbol "<symbolId>" because local <bindingKindLabel> values cannot cross a resume boundary.
codes.why: Lazy symbols run after browser resume. Captures must be graph references, element handles, props/shared values, module imports, or serializable constants.

codes.message: Linked child <missingSymbolSource> does not provide requested symbol module <normalized>. Rebuild the child with the current Markless compiler and clear any stale build cache.

codes.title: children cannot be inspected or transformed
codes.message: children is an opaque template projection: place it with {children}, wrap it, or pass it through — mapping, counting, indexing, or mutating it is not supported.
codes.why: The compiler owns children projection; there is no render-output array to inspect, so React-style children access would silently misbehave.
codes.suggestion: Render {children} directly or move per-item rendering to the parent.

codes.message: <filename> has <length> compiler error(s).

codes.title: Invalid compiler pass graph
Component barrel re-export does not resolve
codes.message: MARKLESS_COMPONENT_BARREL_UNRESOLVED: <filename> re-exports <exportName> from <source>, which does not resolve to a module.
codes.why: A barrel names the parts module rather than the components, so a re-export that resolves to nothing would silently drop every component behind it.
codes.suggestion: Check that <source> exists next to <filename> and is reachable by this build's resolver.

codes.message: <exportName>
"<partName>" is published as a bare render part, not a page.

codes.title: A prop expression that reads state needs a route the child can follow
codes.message: Prop `<propName>` on `<<childComponentName>>` is written as `<source>`, which reads state but is not an expression this compiler can route.
codes.why: A child reads a prop through the graph node the parent named. An expression with no node behind it can only be seeded once, from whatever the value happened to be at render - so the child would show a stale value forever and nothing would say so.
codes.suggestion: Pass a value the compiler can follow: a plain read (`group.value`), or an expression built only from reads, operators and method calls on those reads (`group.value.includes(item.value)`). If the value needs a function of your own, put that function inside a `computed()` and pass the computed.

codes.title: Component root is conditional
codes.message: <componentName> has a second template return, so the public render module cannot choose one component root without deleting statement flow.
codes.why: Initial render executes component bodies, but resume needs one planned root with stable locators. Multiple or conditional template returns need branch records before they can render.
codes.suggestion: Use a single root with @if/@else inside it, or return null before the one root for a guard clause.

codes.title: Only the props rest binding can be spread onto a component
codes.message: `{...<source>}` on `<<childComponentName>>` cannot be forwarded, because `<source>` is not this component's props rest binding.
codes.why: What a spread carries onto a child component is decided at build time, from the signature that produced it. An object assembled anywhere else has no build-time contents, so the child would render without the entries and nothing would say so.
codes.suggestion: Spread the rest binding of this component's own props (`function Part({ known, ...rest })` then `<Child {...rest} />`), or write the props you mean out by name on the tag.

codes.title: Member component tag must come from an import
codes.message: Cannot resolve `<<tagName> />` because `<rootName>` is not imported in this file.
codes.why: The compiler links a child component to the module it comes from at build time. Without an import it cannot find the component to render, and dropping the tag silently would delete the subtree.
codes.suggestion: Import the object that holds the component, for example `import * as <rootName> from './<rootName>.tsrx';` or `import { <rootName> } from './<rootName>.ts';`.

codes.message: DOM update "<recordId>" on host "<hostNodeId>" with symbol "<symbolId>" reads prop "<propName>", but composition found no route.
the compiler cannot tell whether graph node "<graphNodeId>" belongs to a composed component instance or to the page, so it refuses to emit it into the state payload.

codes.title: A computed cannot depend on itself
codes.message: `<initSource>` reads `<name>` — the value it is defining. `<name>` cannot be derived from `<name>`.
codes.why: A derive is a pull-based graph node; a cycle in its dependencies means there is no order in which the graph can produce the value.
codes.suggestion: Reference the source binding you meant to derive from, or rename one of the two values if this was a shadowing typo.

codes.title: A computed() is read as a value, not called ("<called>")
codes.message: <subject> reads "<called>" off its cell, so "<called>" is bound to the value that cell already holds - and the expression spells it "<called>()". Calling a derived value throws a TypeError: <throwsWhen>.
codes.why: computed() answers with the derived VALUE rather than a handle to call - its declared type is the value's own type - so the compiler lowers every read of a computed into a read of its cell. Parentheses written around that read are applied to the value the read answers with, not to the expression that produced it, and nothing at build time pointed at the difference.
codes.suggestion: Drop the parentheses: write "<called>" where the expression writes "<called>()".

codes.title: A computed reads a component-body local the browser cannot recompute
codes.message: `<name>` reads `<localName>`, a local of the component body. The body runs only during the initial render, so the browser's copy of this computed would name a variable that does not exist there.
codes.why: A computed re-derives in the browser from graph reads, props, and module values. A `const` local built only from those is recomputed in place; any other local has no value the browser can reach.
codes.suggestion: Declare `<localName>` as `const <localName> = ...` built only from module values, props, and state; move it to module scope; or make it state: `const <localName> = state(...)`.

codes.title: Rows of a computed() list are read-only
codes.message: Cannot write to "<target>" because "<itemName>" is a row of "<name>", which is a computed() value, and computed() values are read-only.
codes.why: A computed() value is derived from other state every time that state changes, so a change written into one of its rows would have no owner: the next recompute would replace it, and the serialized graph could not say where it belongs after resume.
codes.suggestion: Write the change to <sourceHint> instead, for example by mapping it to a new array: `<list> = <list>.map((item) => (item.id === <itemName>.id ? { ...item, field: value } : item))`. "<name>" recomputes and the row updates.

codes.title: CSS anchoring is regular CSS
codes.message: Cannot write <attributeName> as an attribute. CSS anchoring is regular CSS - declare anchor-name/position-anchor in a <style> block or your stylesheet.
codes.why: An element takes the attributes HTML defines. anchor-name and position-anchor are CSS properties with no HTML attribute of the same name, so nothing on the page would read them.
codes.suggestion: Declare the anchor in a <style> block in this file, or in your stylesheet, and select the element the way you select it for any other style.

codes.title: Element-valued guard returns are not supported
codes.message: <componentName> uses an element-valued guard return before its template root, so the public render plan cannot preserve both outcomes.
codes.why: The public render module needs one planned component root with stable locators. An earlier element-valued return creates another root whose conditional statement flow is not represented by that plan.
codes.suggestion: Rewrite the two outcomes as a root-level @if/@else template, or use return null when the guard should render nothing.

codes.title: element() handle is bound more than once
codes.message: Cannot bind element handle "<handleName>" inside a keyed repeat because one authored handle would point at many row host elements. markless debugging playbook: run pnpm doctor, or read agent/markless.md in the installed @markless/core package
codes.why: Each repeated row has its own DOM locator, so one handle declared as a single element cannot say which row it means.
codes.suggestion: Declare the handle as an ordered set by widening its type argument to an array - element<HTMLElement[]>() - written literally as T[], Array<T> or readonly T[]. Reads then answer every bound element in document order. Otherwise create a separate element() handle for each host element.

codes.title: One element() handle per IDREF attribute
codes.why: The compiler resolves the relationship and the emitter mints the id. Combining handles would require the compiler to spell and order ids it cannot see, and id spelling is not something this record owns.
codes.suggestion: Reference one element() handle directly, as <attributeName>={handle}.

codes.title: An element named by an IDREF cannot also declare an id
codes.message: Cannot mint the id for el={<handleName>} because this element already declares an id attribute.
codes.why: An IDREF position is written from the id the compiler mints for the bound element. A second, authored id on the same element would emit two id attributes and leave the relationship pointing at whichever one the HTML parser kept.
codes.suggestion: Remove the authored id from this element, or drop the element() handle and write the IDREF attribute with your own id string.

codes.title: A repeated element() handle cannot be named by an IDREF
codes.message: Cannot resolve <attributeName>={<source>} because "<handleName>" is bound inside a keyed repeat, so it names one element per row rather than one element.
codes.why: Every row owns its own element and would need its own id. One authored handle cannot name one of them, and picking a row silently would make the relationship point at whichever row happened to render first.
codes.suggestion: Bind a separate element() handle outside the repeat for the element this attribute names, or move the relationship inside the row so each row names its own element.

codes.title: element() handle is referenced but never bound
codes.message: Cannot resolve <attributeName>={<source>} because "<handleName>" is never bound with el={<handleName>} in this component.
codes.why: An IDREF position names another element. With no el={handle} binding there is no element to name, so the compiler would emit an attribute pointing at nothing - a silently broken relationship that renders correctly and helps nobody.
codes.suggestion: Bind the handle to the element it names with el={<handleName>}, or remove the <attributeName> attribute.

codes.title: This shared() element() handle cannot be named by an IDREF here
codes.message: Cannot resolve <attributeName>={<source>} because "<handleName>" is declared in a shared() factory that is not { scope: 'widget' }.
codes.why: A widget-scoped factory is one graph per rendered widget, so the minted id has to carry which widget it belongs to. That token exists for every rendered widget, its root included, and never exists for a page-wide factory.
codes.suggestion: Give the factory { scope: 'widget' } and keep both ends of the relationship inside one rendered widget.

codes.message: Element handle <handleIdOrName> is registered by <registrations> rendered widgets on this page, and the reading handler named no instance. Read the handle from a part of the widget that binds it.

codes.title: An array-typed element() handle cannot fill this position
codes.message: Cannot resolve <attributeName>={<source>} because "<handleName>" is declared as an array (element<T[]>()), so it names an ordered set of elements rather than one.
codes.why: This attribute points at exactly one element. A handle declared with an array type argument may be bound on many elements, and an IDREF carries no order to say which member it means, so the compiler would have to pick one silently.
codes.suggestion: Declare a second, single element() handle for the one element this attribute points at and bind it there, leaving "<handleName>" for the set.

codes.title: Nested prop-forwarded element handles are not supported yet
codes.message: Cannot bind el={<handleName>} because this slice only supports element handles passed as direct component props, not through arrays or nested object props.
codes.why: Direct prop forwarding has one parent-owned element() handle for one child prop. Array and nested object containers need deeper edge tracking before the compiler can prove the owning handle.
codes.suggestion: Pass the element() handle as its own component prop for now, or bind it in the component that renders the host element.

codes.title: DOM handles cannot be read while rendering
codes.message: Cannot render "<source>" because "<handleName>" is an element() handle, not serializable graph state.
codes.why: During initial render the browser DOM element does not exist, and browser resume does not rerun component bodies. Element handles are available to lazy event or behavior code after resume locates the host node.
codes.suggestion: Read DOM properties inside an event handler or attach behavior, and render serializable state() or computed() data instead.

codes.title: el expects an element() handle
codes.message: Cannot bind el={<handleName>} because "<handleName>" is <actual>, not an element() handle.
codes.why: DOM elements are host resources. el can only bind element() handles so resume can recover the current DOM locator without serializing a DOM node.
codes.suggestion: Create a handle with element<T>() and bind that handle with el={handle}. Keep DOM-backed resources in attach={...}.

codes.title: element() handle is read before it is bound
codes.message: Reading element handle "<source>" will produce undefined because "<handleName>" is never bound with el={<handleName>} in this component.
codes.why: element() handles are DOM locator references, not state. A read is only useful after the handle has a host element binding that resume can locate.
codes.suggestion: Bind the handle to one host element with el={handle}, or remove the read if undefined is intentional.

codes.title: element() cannot be created at module scope
codes.message: Cannot create element handle "<name>" at module scope.
codes.why: Element handles are per-render DOM locators. A module-scope handle would be shared across requests and cannot point at one document-owned host element.
codes.suggestion: Move element() creation into the component that owns the host element and bind it with el={handle}.

codes.message: No event record matched <type> dispatch<value>.

codes.title: This event handler cannot run in the browser yet
codes.message: Cannot emit lazy <kind> symbol "<symbolId>" because it reads component-local "<name>", a local <bindingKindLabel> value that cannot cross a resume boundary.
codes.why: Lazy handler symbols run after browser resume. Handler bodies may use graph references, element handles, props/shared values, module imports, or serializable capture-plane inputs; unsupported body locals would otherwise become silent no-op code.

codes.title: Event props need a function
codes.message: `<attributeName>={<source>}` passes the result of `<source>`, not a function. The expression would run once while rendering, and the click would receive a number.
codes.why: An event prop compiles to a lazy handler symbol that runs on the browser event; only a function can be that handler.
codes.suggestion: Wrap it in a function, for example <attributeName>={() => <source>}.

codes.title: Event handlers cannot be spread onto an element
codes.message: {...<spreadSource>} spreads <listed> onto an element. Events compile to static view records, so handlers inside a spread would be discarded.
codes.why: The compiler owns event discovery so the browser can resume without scanning markup; a runtime spread hides which events exist from the compiler.
codes.suggestion: Write event props directly, for example <input onClick={handlers.onClick} onInput={handlers.onInput} />, and keep spreads for plain static attributes.

codes.title: Framework APIs cannot be aliased or passed as values
codes.message: `<declarationKind> <localName> = <apiName>` copies the framework API `<apiName>` into a plain variable. `<localName>(5)` would not create graph state — the compiler only rewrites calls made through the imported name.
codes.why: <apiName>() is compiled away into graph cells; it has no runtime function value that an alias could call.
codes.suggestion: Call the imported API directly — before: `const makeState = state; let x = makeState(5);` — after: `let x = state(5);`. For a reusable initialization pattern, wrap the VALUE, not the API (`const defaults = () => ({ open: false }); const menu = state(defaults());`).

codes.title: Framework API executed without compiler output
codes.why: �0�() is an markless framework API that must be rewritten by the .tsrx compiler before runtime execution.

codes.title: Framework API must be imported
codes.message: `<callSource>` calls your local function `<apiName>`, but in `.tsrx` files `<apiName>` is a compiler-recognized markless API name. Rename the local function, or import the framework API from `@markless/core`.
codes.why: The compiler recognizes `state`/`computed`/`element`/`shared`/`storage` by name in `.tsrx` reactive scopes so that graph ownership stays unambiguous for readers and tools.
codes.suggestion: Rename the helper (before: `function <apiName>(value) { ... }` — after: `function doubleValue(value) { ... }`), or, if graph state was intended, delete the helper and add `import { <apiName> } from '@markless/core';`.

codes.title: A handler reads a component-body local the browser cannot recompute
codes.message: The `<handlerLabel>` handler reads `<localName>`, a local of the component body. The body runs only during the initial render, so the browser copy of this handler would name a variable that does not exist there.
codes.why: A handler runs in the browser from graph reads, props, and module values. A `const` local built only from those is recomputed in place; any other local has no value the browser can reach.
codes.suggestion: Declare `<localName>` as `const <localName> = ...` built only from module values, props, and state; move it to module scope; or make it state: `const <localName> = state(...)`.

codes.title: Imported child has no published symbol claims
codes.message: MARKLESS_IMPORTED_SYMBOL_CLAIMS_MISSING: Parent module <parent> composes imported child <specifier>, whose symbols must be bound by the parent, but the child's symbol claims were not published when the parent linked it.
codes.why: Linking without the child claims silently drops the parent-bound symbol rows, so the child handlers would not resolve after resume.
codes.suggestion: This is a linker ordering defect: the child must finish compiling in this environment before its parent links it.

codes.message: Source <source> could not seal imported symbol claims after final publications.

codes.title: This list can never grow in the browser
codes.message: <message> The browser has no renderer, so a row that arrives after the page loads has no markup to be built from: this list will render the rows the server sent, reorder them and remove them, and silently ignore every new one.
codes.why: The payload carries one row of finished markup so the browser can build a row the server never rendered. It can fill text and attributes read off the row item or off a state cell the page holds, and nothing else, so a row needing anything more ships no template at all.

codes.message: linked render-data wake must not read markless/state or markless/view payload scripts.
<componentIndex>
<componentIndex>

codes.title: This module-scope instance would become one instance per handler
codes.message: Module-scope instance "<name>" is carried into <length> handler modules (<symbolIds>). Each of those modules runs its own constructor, so they hold <length> separate instances and anything one of them records is invisible to the others.
codes.why: Every handler symbol module is loaded on its own when its handler first fires, so a declaration in the authoring file has to be copied into each one that names it. One handler gets the intended browser-side instance. Two or more get a copy each, and nothing at runtime reveals that they have drifted apart.
codes.suggestion: Move "<name>" and its class into their own module and import it. An import resolves to one module instance that every handler module shares, so the handlers agree.

codes.title: overlay can only be marked on host elements
codes.message: Cannot mark overlay on component <owner>. overlay elevates one concrete host element above the rest of the UI and needs a host element owner.
codes.why: Elevation is applied to a DOM element. A component is not a DOM locator and may render zero, one, or many host nodes, and overlay cannot be forwarded to one as a prop because its value must be a literal.
codes.suggestion: Move overlay onto the host element that should be elevated, inside the component TSRX body.

codes.title: overlay accepts only a literal
codes.message: <bound>. overlay must be written on the element itself as bare `overlay`, `overlay={true}`, or `overlay={false}`.
codes.why: Elevation is structural, not reactive. The overlay record carries no inputs, so it has no dependencies and can never re-run; a value that varies at runtime would have nothing to re-elevate the element.
codes.suggestion: Let `@if` decide whether the element exists and keep `overlay` a literal on the element inside the branch.

codes.title: This list is projected into a hole that repeats
codes.message: The @for over `<collectionSource>` is written inside <child>'s children, and <child> renders its `{children}` inside its own @for row, so the list would be painted once per row and has no single element to grow in.
codes.why: A keyed repeat records one parent element: resume keys the served rows under it and inserts new rows into it. A hole inside a repeated row renders the projection once per row, so there is no one element the record could name, and the rows would silently never update.
codes.suggestion: Move the @for into a component of its own and render that component inside <child>'s row, or lift the list above <child>.

codes.title: This component root cannot be rendered yet
codes.message: No component with a TSRX template root was found, so the compiled module would render nothing.
codes.why: Markless anchors each component's HTML and interactivity to a single root element. Without a supported root the component would silently render nothing, so the compiler stops with an error instead.
codes.suggestion: Export a TSRX component with an @{...} template body, or pass an explicit compiled component artifact when multiple roots exist.

codes.why: Component bodies execute during initial render. A body statement the emitter cannot represent would otherwise be deleted from CSR and SSR output.

codes.title: Render data links a scoped style module the link does not carry
codes.message: MARKLESS_RENDER_DATA_STYLE_UNLINKED: Render data for <source> links scoped style module <styleModule>, which this link does not carry.
codes.why: A scoped style that is compiled but never linked ships a component whose markup renders unstyled in the consuming app, with nothing at build time to show it went missing.
codes.suggestion: Register the scoped style virtual module alongside the render-data module it belongs to before the link is read.

codes.title: Two @for loops give the same name two different meanings
codes.message: "<name>" is one @for loop's item and another @for loop's index in the same file. Rename one of them.
codes.why: Every @for expression in a file is compiled into readers that share one set of row bindings, so a name can bind to the row item or the row index, never to both.
codes.suggestion: Rename this loop's binding - two loops may reuse a name freely as long as both use it the same way (both items, or both indexes).

codes.title: This @for collection reaches no cell on its shared instance
codes.message: @for (const <itemName> of <collectionSource>) reads through `<rootName>`, a shared instance local of this component, but `<collectionSource>` resolves to no graph cell. `<rootName>` exists only inside the component function, so the rows would be taken from an expression that names nothing where the repeat renders.
codes.why: Rows come from a reactive graph read; a shared-instance path that resolves to no cell leaves the repeat with an authored expression whose receiver is undeclared in the emitted scope, which throws on the first server render.
codes.suggestion: Return the cell as a property of a spread object from the shared factory, so `<collectionSource>` names a graph cell. Before: `shared(() => { const box = state({ items: [] }); return box; })`; after: `shared(() => { const box = state({ items: [] }); return { ...box }; })`.

codes.title: Two rows share the same @for key
codes.message: Duplicate @for key <keyText> from <source>.
codes.why: The key is each row identity across reorder, insert, delete, and resume; duplicate identities make row state and DOM ownership ambiguous.

codes.title: Keying by index makes row identity follow the position
codes.message: key <indexName> identifies each row of <collectionSource> by its position, not by its data. If <collectionSource> reorders, inserts, or deletes, any row-local state, event wiring, and DOM reuse stay with the slot number.
codes.why: The key is the identity root for a repeated graph scope; a positional key pins that scope to the slot, which is only correct when state genuinely belongs to the position.
codes.suggestion: Key by a stable field of the item when state belongs to the item, such as `@for (const <itemName> of <collectionSource>; key <itemName>.id)`. Keep `key <indexName>` when state should follow the slot.

codes.title: This @for needs a key
codes.message: @for (const <itemName> of <collectionSource>) repeats reactive state without a key. When <collectionSource> changes, the rows of this list have no identity to update, reorder, or resume by.
codes.why: A keyed loop item keeps its state, events, and DOM attached to the same logical item across reorder, insert, and delete; without a key there is no stable identity root.
codes.suggestion: Add a stable domain key such as `@for (const <itemName> of <collectionSource>; key <itemName>.id)`, or key by position with `index i; key i` when state should follow the slot.

codes.title: @for key must identify the item stably
codes.message: key <keySource> does not derive identity from <itemName> or an explicit index alias. Row state, event wiring, and DOM reuse follow the key, so rows of <collectionSource> could not be matched with themselves reliably.
codes.why: The key is the stable identity root for a repeated graph scope across reorder, insert, delete, and resume; a value that is not derived from the item or its position cannot identify anything.
codes.suggestion: Key by a stable field of <itemName>, such as `key <itemName>.id`, or key by position with `index i; key i` when state should follow the slot.

codes.title: This @for renders its rows once and never updates them
codes.message: @for (const <itemName> of <collectionSource>) takes its rows from `<rootName>`, which is neither a state cell nor a computed, so the repeat resolves to no graph node and its rows are built on the server and never rebuilt in the browser. The row body reads `<readSource>`, a <value> that can change after that render, and those rows would silently keep their first-render values.
codes.why: A keyed repeat reconciles through the graph node its collection resolves to; a collection that resolves to none renders its rows once, so any reactive read inside a row is frozen at its first-render value with nothing said at build time.
codes.suggestion: Put the collection on the graph - `const <rootName> = state([...])` or `const <rootName> = computed(() => ...)` inside the component - so the rows rebuild when `<readSource>` changes; or keep the rows static by reading only `<itemName>` inside them.

codes.suggestion: Rebuild the owning module so both publications claim the same set.

codes.title: roster count is spent as a number before the page can answer it
codes.message: Cannot spend the roster count "<computedName>" in <operation> ("<source>") in <componentName>: at server render the count is a placeholder the renderer resolves once the page has composed, so only a bare read printed as text or as an attribute value carries it.<arrivedAs>
codes.why: A count is how many parts END UP in the family instance, and a single forward render pass cannot know that when the asker renders. The render writes a placeholder and the served page answers every one it wrote, which a printed value carries and an operation destroys - the comparison or the arithmetic runs against the placeholder string and paints a wrong value silently.
codes.suggestion: Print <computedName> on its own - {<computedName>}, an attribute value, or a ${<computedName>} slot in a template literal - and do the arithmetic in an event handler or in CSS, where the count is a number.

codes.title: Client route artifact registered after its primary module transformed
codes.message: MARKLESS_ROUTE_ARTIFACT_REGISTERED_LATE: Client route artifact <source> was registered after its primary module transformed. Register every production route artifact before transformation begins.
codes.why: The primary module has already been compiled without knowing it composes a route artifact, so its emitted graph would be wrong.
codes.suggestion: Register every production route artifact before transformation begins.

<<componentName>> inside a @for row keyed by position has its own state, events, or async content, so its interactions cannot resume: an index key carries no row value to route them to. Key the @for by a stable field of the item, or keep components in index-keyed rows presentational (markup from item props, like <Link>).

codes.title: This is not a row-ownable element() handle
codes.message: Cannot bind el={<handleName>} inside <element>. A row host takes a declared element() handle, named directly (el={row}) or as one member off a shared() instance (el={select.optionEls}). markless debugging playbook: run pnpm doctor, or read agent/markless.md in the installed @markless/core package
codes.why: The keyed row record owns one host slot per authored handle and repeat key. Forwarded props, deeper paths, and nested repeat scopes do not identify one compiler-proven row-owned slot.
codes.suggestion: Declare the handle with const row = element<HTMLElement[]>() in this component or in the shared() factory the row reads, then bind el={row} - or el={family.row} - directly on the keyed row host.

codes.title: These children cannot be seeded into shared state
codes.message: <<componentName>> seeds "<statePath>" from its children, but the children written here contain a value that is worked out while they render, so the seed would read nothing.
codes.why: Shared state is seeded before the projected children render, because those children render from what the seed wrote. Only children the consumer passes as a prop, and children the compiler already spells in full - text, or markup with no expression in it - are known that early.
codes.suggestion: Write the value as a prop (children={...}), or put text between the tags with no expression in it, or move the write into an event handler where the shared instance is already live.

codes.title: Cannot serialize graph state value
codes.message: Cannot serialize value at <cellPrefix> because unknown values are not durable graph state.
codes.why: Serialization is for durable graph state. Functions and host/runtime resources cannot be restored during resume.
codes.suggestion: Move runtime resources into attach={...}, make the value serializable state, or derive it with computed().

codes.title: This computed value cannot be worked out on the server
codes.message: <cause> Anything reading it would render as if the value were missing.
codes.why: Server rendering works each computed value out once and puts it in the state the page is served with. A value it cannot work out reads as undefined, and every attribute and piece of text built from it silently disappears from the HTML.
codes.suggestion: cycle

codes.title: a shared() call must be bound to a name
codes.message: shared() definition "<definitionName>" is called but its result is discarded.
codes.why: Reads and writes of a shared instance resolve through the name the call was bound to. An unbound call names nothing, so it lowers to no client behavior while the server render still tries to run it and throws.
codes.suggestion: Bind the call and read through the name: `<binding>`.

codes.message: <name> — a shared definition can only be called from a compiled module; this call site was not compiled.

codes.title: Shared definition call does not resolve
codes.message: `<callSource>` reaches no shared() definition. <resolves>
codes.why: A call the compiler cannot resolve to a shared() definition creates no graph instance, so every read of it would render a dead value and every write would go nowhere — silently, at runtime.
codes.suggestion: Export the definition from the module this call names, and compile that module in this build. Before: `export const famState = shared(() => ..., { scope: 'widget' })` in `fam.tsrx` with nothing re-exporting it; after: `export { famState as state } from './fam.tsrx';` in the family index, so `fam.state()` names it.

codes.title: A shared() computed cannot be read from another module yet ("<name>")
codes.message: Serving this page works "<name>" out by copying its expression from <definedIn> into this file. The copied expression names "<name>", which <definedIn> means as its own, and THIS file already binds "<name>" as <text>; one module scope cannot hold both, and matched against it by name alone the served value would be built from this module's "<name>" rather than the one <definedIn> means.
codes.why: A shared() factory has no instance on the server to ask for a computed value, so the server works the value out by copying the factory's own expression into the module of every page that reads it. The imports and module-scope constants that expression names travel with the definition and are emitted beside the copy, but a name this file already binds from somewhere else cannot be: the emitted module would bind it twice, and matching by name alone would build the served value from this module's value instead.
codes.suggestion: Rename this module's "<name>", or import it under another local name, so the one <definedIn> means can be carried in beside the copy.

codes.title: Shared definitions cannot depend on each other circularly
codes.message: Cannot create shared definition cycle "<cycleSource>".
codes.why: shared() instances are created from graph context during initial render and resume. A cycle would require one shared instance before its own dependency graph can be created.
codes.suggestion: Break the shared() dependency cycle by passing plain data between definitions or by moving the shared read into an event method that runs after instance creation.

codes.message: <name>

codes.title: A shared() factory cannot return a class instance
codes.message: shared() definition "<name>" returns <constructorName>, so the definition declares no fields at all: the payload carries nothing for it, and both the server render and the browser handler name a value that was never built.
codes.why: A shared() factory declares the graph fields the payload carries and the server render rebuilds. A class instance declares none, so every read of it is a reference to a binding that does not exist in the module doing the reading.
codes.suggestion: Return a plain object instead: the durable data becomes fields, and the behaviour becomes methods on the same object (`shared(() => ({ index: 0, next() { ... } }))`).

codes.title: shared() family has no declared scope
codes.message: <length> components in this module resolve shared() "<definitionName>" (<components>), which is the shape of a widget family, but no scope is declared so it is page-scoped.
codes.why: A page-scoped family gives every widget of that family on one page the same graph, so two of them move together. That is a real choice, but silence makes it a surprise.
codes.suggestion: Add { scope: 'widget' } to give each rendered widget its own graph.

codes.title: The exported function "<name>" resolves a shared() definition at module scope
codes.message: "<name>" is exported from this file and calls `<definitionName>()` in its body. A shared() instance is resolved by a component as it renders, and this function is not a component, so there is no instance for the call to return. Compiling this file drops the `export` keyword from "<name>" and carries the rest into the emitted symbol modules, where `<definitionName>` is not carried at all — the definition ships as payload graph nodes rather than as code. The copy that lands would throw the moment it runs, and the export a consumer imported is gone.
codes.why: A shared() definition is graph data, not module code: its factory is compiled into payload nodes and the runtime resolves a property of it only for a component instance that asked for one. That makes a component body the only place a resolving call means anything. An exported plain function is neither carried with its definition nor reachable as a part, so the compiler would have to silently publish less than the file says it publishes.
codes.suggestion: Make "<name>" a part this family publishes — a component whose body resolves `<definitionName>()` — and compose it where the behavior is wanted.

codes.title: Shared state has no such member
codes.message: Cannot read "<source>" because the <definitionName>() shared state declares no member named "<member>".
codes.why: A member read is lowered into a path subscription on a declared graph node. A path the node never declares reads undefined on every render and after resume, so the code that depends on it silently does nothing.
codes.suggestion: Declare "<member>" in the state() initial value of <definitionName>(), or read a member the definition already declares.

codes.title: A shared() method cannot be called from another module yet (<shared>)
codes.message: The emitted <kind> module for <symbolId> was built by copying the body of <shared> out of <files> into this file. <where> <what>
codes.why: Calling a shared() method compiles to copying the method's authored body into the calling handler, because no shared instance exists inside a handler module to call the method on. Copying text moves the statements but not the scope they were written in, so the copy only means what the author wrote while the definition and the call are in one file. Across files the definition module's imports and module-scope declarations do not travel, and the calling module's imports are matched against the copied text by name, which can capture a same-named binding that means something else entirely. Both failures are invisible until the gesture runs, so this build refuses instead.
codes.suggestion: Call <value> from a part the family itself publishes, in <files>, and compose that part here. Inside its own module the same call compiles and runs today.

codes.title: a shared() factory must return named state
codes.message: shared() definition "<definitionName>" returns <apiName>() directly, so the cells it returns have no name.
codes.why: A shared() cell is serialized under an id spelled from the name it was declared with, and every read of the instance resolves through that id. An inline call in return position declares no name, so no node exists, and each read of the instance falls back to the authored text and throws at render.
codes.suggestion: Name the cells and return the name: `const s = <apiName>(...); return s;`.

codes.title: shared() scope must be valid
codes.message: Unknown shared() scope <valueText>. Valid scopes are <valid>.
codes.why: shared() scope controls graph lifetime. Silently dropping an unknown scope changes whether data is request, container, page, or widget owned.
codes.suggestion: Use `shared(factory, { scope: "request" })`, `shared(factory, { scope: "container" })`, `shared(factory, { scope: "page" })`, or `shared(factory, { scope: "widget" })`.

codes.title: Shared instance has no such field to seed
codes.message: Cannot write to "<target>" because "<definitionName>()" declares no graph field named "<field>". Instance callback fields such as "<field>" are not supported yet (tracked).
codes.why: A component body seed is lowered into an initial value for a graph node the shared definition declared. With no matching node there is nothing to seed, and the authored assignment cannot run on the server because the emitted body keeps no local for the shared instance.
codes.suggestion: Return "<field>" from the <definitionName>() factory as state() or computed() graph data, or pass the callback to the component as a prop and call it from an event handler.

codes.title: a shared() seed value has nothing to bind to
codes.message: The state() seed for "<fieldName>" in shared() definition "<definitionName>" is `<valueSource>`, and "<freeName>" is not a literal, a module-scope declaration of this file, an import, or a global.
codes.why: A factory seed is re-evaluated in a module of its own, carrying only this file's module scope and imports. A name that is none of those has nothing to bind to there, so the seed throws a ReferenceError and the whole shape loses its fields — which then reads as an error at every consumer of the shape rather than here.
codes.suggestion: Seed "<fieldName>" with a literal, or with a module-scope `const` of this file that "<freeName>" can resolve to.

codes.title: Cannot seed shared state from this expression
codes.message: Cannot seed "<target>" from "<target>" because a component body seeds a shared instance only from its own props or from constants.
codes.why: A component body runs once during initial render. The compiler turns a shared-state assignment there into a per-instance initial value, which it can only build from values the render already has: this component's props and constants.
codes.suggestion: Assign a prop or a constant, or move the write into an event handler where the shared instance is already live.

codes.title: Emitted symbol claims for one source disagree
codes.message: MARKLESS_SOURCE_SYMBOL_CLAIMS_DIVERGED: Source <source> has incompatible emitted symbol claims in <firstOwner> and <secondOwner>.
codes.why: Merging contradictory claims would let one emitted sibling silently redefine a symbol another sibling already routes to.
codes.suggestion: Rebuild the source so every emitted sibling publishes the same rows for a shared symbol, and clear any stale build cache.

codes.message: Source <source> published final claims without an active emitted variant.
Source <source> claims were consumed before final publication completed. Emitted variants that have not published: <unpublished>.

codes.title: Spread attributes render once
codes.message: {...<spreadSource>} copies attributes during initial render. When <spreadSource> changes later, these attributes do not update.
codes.why: The compiler plans DOM-update records for graph-backed attributes it can see; a spread hides which attributes exist, so no update records are planned for it.
codes.suggestion: Bind attributes that change individually, such as <div id={menu.id} data-open={menu.open} />, and keep the spread only for initial attributes.

codes.title: Cannot reassign a const graph binding
codes.message: Cannot update "<target>" because it was declared with const. JavaScript const binding semantics are preserved for state().
codes.why: state() removes marker syntax, but it does not change JavaScript binding rules. A const binding cannot be reassigned during resume or initial render.
codes.suggestion: Use let for scalar state you reassign, or mutate a property path on object state such as menu.open.

codes.title: state() and computed() need a stable creation site
codes.message: <apiName>() creates "<name>" <message>. That would ship a graph cell whose identity does not match when this code runs.
codes.why: <why> Graph cells are planned into the payload before rendering, so each authored declaration needs one stable component-body or shared owner.

codes.title: Imported module-scope state is not resumable
codes.message: Cannot import graph state "<importedName>" from "<sourceModule>" into "<filename>".
codes.why: Module-scope state has no per-request graph ownership. Importing it would compile reads as dead snapshots and writes as plain module mutation instead of connecting to this document payload.
codes.suggestion: Move the state() call into the component that owns it, or expose request/container/page lifetime data with shared() and import that shared() definition instead.

codes.title: Graph destructuring defaults are not supported yet
codes.message: Cannot create graph alias "<localName>" from "<target>" with a default value.
codes.why: A destructuring default must run only when the property value is undefined. The current graph alias artifact can represent a graph path, but not a fallback expression without changing JavaScript semantics.
codes.suggestion: Use an explicit computed() for fallback logic, or read the graph path directly without a destructuring default.

codes.title: Cannot read from a dynamic graph path
codes.message: Cannot read "<source>" because graph read paths must be statically resolvable.
codes.why: The resumable state graph records path-level subscriptions in the payload. A dynamic property expression cannot be represented as a stable graph subscription by the current compiler pass.
codes.suggestion: Use a statically named property path, a literal array index, or model the dynamic lookup as a computed() with explicit compiler support.

codes.title: Cannot write to a dynamic graph path
codes.message: Cannot write to "<target>" because graph write paths must be statically resolvable.
codes.why: The resumable state graph records path-level writes in the payload and runtime journal. A dynamic property expression cannot be represented as a stable graph path by the current compiler pass.
codes.suggestion: Use a statically named property path, a literal array index, or a collection method with compiler coverage for this state update.

codes.title: element() handles cannot be stored in state
codes.message: Cannot store element handle "<handleName>" in state "<stateName>" because element handles are DOM locators, not serializable graph data.
codes.why: state() values are serialized into markless/state and resumed without running component bodies. An element() handle resolves through DOM locator metadata and must stay outside serialized graph state.
codes.suggestion: Keep element handles in element() bindings and bind them with el={handle}. Store serializable ids, flags, or data in state() instead.

codes.title: Helper-created state return shape is not supported
codes.message: <apiName>() creates "<name>" inside a helper function, but the compiler cannot connect this helper return shape to the component graph binding.
codes.why: The compiler supports same-module direct helper returns and compiled imported helpers. This gate remains for residual helper shapes such as object returns, nested return chains, or imported helpers without module graph interface data.
codes.suggestion: Return the graph binding directly from the helper, compile the imported helper with interface output, or declare the state in the component body.

codes.title: Module-scope storage cannot be written from render or handlers
codes.message: Cannot write to "<target>"<aliasText>.
codes.why: Module-scope storage outlives a single server render. A handler could read or overwrite data from another user because the value is not part of this document payload.
codes.suggestion: Keep per-document values inside state(), or use shared() for named request/container/page dataflow instead of module variables.

codes.title: state() and computed() cannot be created at module scope
codes.message: Cannot create "<name>" with <callName>() at module scope.
codes.why: Module-scope graph state would be shared across requests and has no per-document serialization payload.
codes.suggestion: Move state() or computed() creation into a component or declare request/container/page state with shared().

codes.title: state() cannot be the initial value of another state()
codes.message: `<initSource>` declares graph state whose initial value is another state() call. `<name>` cannot store graph state as its value.
codes.why: A graph cell serializes plain data across the resume boundary; a state() call declares a cell and has no serializable value form.
codes.suggestion: Before: `const x = state(state(5));` — After: `const x = state(5);`.

codes.title: Cannot write graph state through optional chaining
codes.message: Cannot write to "<target>" through optional chaining because graph writes must have definite targets.
codes.why: Optional chaining can skip the method call and its arguments at runtime. The current graph write artifact cannot preserve that short-circuit behavior safely across resume.
codes.suggestion: Guard explicitly before mutating graph state, or initialize the state path so the collection method call always has a definite target.

codes.title: A class instance cannot be a field of a shared() or state() value
codes.why: Only declared graph fields cross the boundary. A class instance is not one, so the rebuilt object has a hole where the field was, and any method reached through the graph arrives unbound.
codes.suggestion: Make the durable data plain fields on the same object, and put the behaviour beside them as methods (`{ index: 0, next() { ... } }`).

codes.title: Cannot write to a read-only graph binding
codes.message: Cannot write to "<target>" because <bindingLabel> are read-only.

codes.title: Per-row state in keyed repeats is not supported yet
codes.message: <apiName>() creates "<name>" inside a keyed @for row. Per-row cells need per-row graph scopes, which do not exist yet.
codes.why: Keys give rows identity, but each row would need its own cell keyed by row identity across reorder and resume. The current graph payload can only plan stable component-owned cells.
codes.suggestion: Lift the state to a collection on the parent: use one state() holding per-row data keyed by the row key.

codes.title: Cannot write through an object-rest excluded path
codes.message: Cannot write to "<source>" because "<excludedPathSource>" was excluded when "<aliasName>" was created.
codes.why: Object rest destructuring creates an alias for the remaining graph paths only. Paths explicitly destructured out of the source object are not owned by the rest alias.
codes.suggestion: Write through the original graph path, or use the explicit destructured alias for the excluded property.

codes.title: Handler write would leave the template stale
codes.message: Cannot write to "<target>" from a handler because the template reads the component local "<name>" only during initial render.
codes.why: Component bodies run for initial render only. Template reads re-render after events only when they subscribe through state(), so this handler write would leave the UI stale after resume.
codes.suggestion: Move "<name>" into state(), then write <name>++ so Markless can serialize the cell and update subscribed DOM.

codes.title: Host-object write is not tracked as state
codes.message: The write to "<target>" runs imperatively, but Markless does not track it as graph state.
codes.why: Member-expression writes can update host objects at runtime, but they do not produce resumable state graph updates.
codes.suggestion: Declare the local before writing it, or move UI-changing values into state() so Markless can serialize and resume the update.

codes.title: A computed cannot write graph state
codes.message: `<source>` writes to `<target>` while deriving a computed value. A computed is a graph read, so writing graph state there would re-trigger the same derivation.
codes.why: A computed is a demand-driven read in the graph; the only effects in the system are compiler-generated DOM updates, so a write inside a derive is a self-waking cycle that cannot resume.
codes.suggestion: Keep computed() pure. Move graph writes to an event handler and derive only from graph reads.

codes.title: Cannot write state inside a template expression
codes.why: DOM updates are the only effects in the demand-driven graph; a write inside a branch test creates a self-waking cycle that cannot resume.
codes.suggestion: Render the value directly and move the mutation to an event handler or another explicit write site.

codes.title: Storage key must be static
codes.message: storage(key, fallback) requires an explicit key to be a static string literal; omit it to derive markless:<identifier>.
codes.why: The compiler bakes the key into a stable graph identity and storage key at compile time; it cannot be a runtime value.
codes.suggestion: Pass a string literal, for example `storage('theme', 'light')`, or omit the key: `storage('light')`.

codes.message: <graphNodeId> has no static string fallback.
Async boundary <boundaryId> settled during streaming, but the re-render pass produced no <expected> in its <where>. The settled @try/@catch content cannot stream.

codes.title: This style object shape is not supported
codes.message: style={<valueSource>} uses <reason>, which style objects do not support. Supported: an object literal written on the element, or an unmodified same-file `const` object literal referenced by name or flattened with `...spread`, with keys that are plain names or compile-time strings and values that are literals, state, computed values, or props.
codes.why: A style object is turned into CSS text while compiling, so every key must be readable from the source and every value must be one the compiler can recombine into the same text the server renders and the browser rewrites. Objects that are imported, held in state, mutated, aliased, or built at runtime cannot be frozen that way.
codes.suggestion: Write the declarations directly on the element, such as style={{ color: theme, marginTop: 8 }}, move the object into an unmodified same-file const, or pass a CSS string.

codes.title: TSRX submodules are not supported by this host yet
codes.message: module-block
codes.why: TSRX defines submodule syntax but defers boundary semantics to the host. Until markless implements splitting, treating this as supported would silently ship server-intended code to the client.
codes.suggestion: Move the code into a separate module with a string import specifier, or wait for the submodule host boundary decision in specs/framework/08-deferred-decisions.md.

codes.title: This expression reads "<name>" in a shape the compiler cannot lower
codes.message: The emitted <kind> module for <symbolId> still names "<name>" directly. <where> "<name>" is a state binding that lives in the component, not in the handler module, so this module would throw a ReferenceError the first time it runs.
codes.why: A handler is compiled into a module of its own and every read of state has to be rewritten into a graph read. When an expression nests a state read under a call — `s.text.slice(0, 3).length` — the rewrite has no name for the value it would read, so nothing is rewritten and the authored text is emitted as it stands. Shipping that module would move a build-time gap into a runtime crash on the first click.
codes.suggestion: Read the state into a local first, then use the local: `const value = <name>.<field>;` on its own line, and build the expression out of `value`. A local read is lowered, and everything after it is plain JavaScript.

codes.message: <type> <normalizedId> was loaded before its owner <ownerSource> published a final compile.

codes.title: Only one cancel statement becomes the synchronous event policy
codes.message: This <action>() for <attributeName> sits outside the statement the synchronous policy was extracted from, so it would run only after the lazy handler loads and never reach the event.
codes.why: The compiler lifts one guarded cancel per handler into the policy the resumer applies before the handler symbol loads; every other cancel stays in the lazy handler, where the event has already finished dispatching.
codes.suggestion: Fold the guards into one extractable condition, e.g. `if (first || second) <eventParam>.<action>()`, or remove the extra <action>().

codes.title: Cannot extract synchronous event policy
codes.message: `<source>` detaches <action> from the event, so the compiler cannot prove when the default action is cancelled for <attributeName>.
codes.why: preventDefault() and stopPropagation() must run before lazy handler symbols load; a detached reference hides which action runs and under what condition.
codes.suggestion: Call it directly on the event parameter instead of detaching <action>.

codes.title: A template is not a value
codes.message: <siteSource> puts a template<target> where Markless needs runtime data. Templates compile into page structure with locators, not values to store, pass, or serialize.
codes.why: Markless has no VDOM. Templates compile to DOM structure and resume locators, so there is no render-output object that can live in state, a computed value, a local variable, or an array.
codes.suggestion: Keep templates in the tree. Use @if/@for for conditional or repeated structure, extract child components for reusable structure, or pass nested content through children projection.

codes.title: This expression reads state but never updates
codes.message: This text reads `<readSource>`, but only plain reads like `{<readSource>}` update the page today. The expression renders its initial value and never changes when `<readSource>` changes.
codes.why: Each template read compiles to a graph subscription with a DOM-update record; composite expressions are not lowered yet, so no subscription exists to wake this text.
codes.suggestion:
Hoist the logic into a derived value: `const label = computed(() => a ? 'x' : 'y');` with `

{label}

`.

codes.title: A markup expression that reads state needs a route the page can follow
codes.message: <target> is written as `<source>`, which reads state but is not an expression this compiler can keep current.
codes.why: An expression with no graph node behind it renders once, from whatever the value was at render, and a later write never reaches it - so the page would show a stale value and nothing would say so.
codes.suggestion: Write a plain read (`group.value`), or an expression built only from reads, operators and method calls on those reads. If the value needs a function of your own, put that function inside a `computed()` and read the computed here.

codes.title: Template read is not declared in render scope
codes.why: Public CSR and SSR render modules execute template expressions directly during initial render. An identifier that is not declared in the emitted render scope would crash instead of rendering HTML.
codes.suggestion: Declare <name> in the component body, pass it as a prop, import it, or hoist it to a module-scope declaration before reading it in the template.

codes.title: Toggling this <branchLabel> re-renders the whole @try block
codes.why: Content with a component cannot be rebuilt from static parts and value slots, so the toggle falls back to re-rendering the whole @try block. That works, but it re-runs the component and replaces DOM the toggle did not touch.
codes.suggestion: Move the component outside the <branchLabel>, or keep the <branchLabel> content to plain elements, text, and state reads.

codes.title: @markless/ui value imports must use named exports from the package root
codes.message: Line <line> imports from `<importSource>` with an unsupported shape; <fix>.
codes.why: Application value imports from a family subpath or a namespace can expose source files to dependency optimization instead of using the package root export surface.
codes.suggestion: Replace this declaration: <fix>.

codes.message: <graphNodeId> was read at dispatch from a part whose widget instance no rendered widget owns, so the read would answer for no instance at all.
